s: A. State action.
The Fourteenth Amendment says "No State shall…," and most constitutional rights restrain government, not private persons.
In the Civil Rights Cases (1883), the Court struck down the public-accommodations provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1875 because § 5 reaches only state action.
The Thirteenth Amendment is the exception: it applies to private conduct.
Private conduct may nevertheless be attributed to the state.
When is private conduct state action?
Public function.
The private actor performs a function "traditionally and exclusively" reserved to the state, such as running elections (Terry v. Adams) or a company town (Marsh v. Alabama, 1946).
Merely operating a public-access channel (Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck, 2019) or a school receiving public funds (Rendell-Baker v. Kohn) does not qualify.
Entanglement and joint participation.

A symbiotic relationship exists (Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority, 1961), the state is entwined in management (Brentwood Academy, 2001), or the state jointly participates (Lugar v. Edmondson Oil, prejudgment attachment).
Coercion or significant encouragement.
The state compels or significantly encourages the private choice (Blum v. Yaretsky).
Government pressure on private speech intermediaries can violate the First Amendment (NRA v. Vullo, 2024), though standing problems are common (Murthy v. Missouri).
Judicial enforcement.
Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) held that court enforcement of racially restrictive covenants is state action.
The principle has not been extended generally.
Officials on social media.
A public official's speech is state action only if the official had actual authority to speak for the state and purported to exercise it (Lindke v. Freed, 2024).
Regulation, licensing, or public funding alone is not enough (Jackson v. Metropolitan Edison, 1974; Moose Lodge v. Irvis, 1972).
Congress may reach private conduct through other powers, notably the Commerce Clause (Civil Rights Act of 1964) and § 2 of the Thirteenth Amendment.
